rationale: Comprehensive evaluation of the available cohort data confirms that dystonia is the primary, near-universal movement disorder in bi-allelic ACBD6 deficiency, documented in 94% (42/45) of affected individuals in the definitive discovery cohort (Kaiyrzhanov et al., 2024; PMC10994533). In contrast, classical chorea is not prominent; while review literature categorizes ACBD6 under chorea syndromes or mentions chorea-like jerky movements (likely representing the jerky tremor or myoclonic/dystonic jerks observed in 59-63% of patients), dystonia and tremor markedly predominate across reported clinical evaluations.

evidence.text: In the discovery cohort of 45 affected individuals from 28 unrelated families with bi-allelic ACBD6 mutations, dystonia was reported as the most conspicuous and common movement disorder present in 94% of cases, alongside postural deformities in 97%, limb dystonia in 55%, cervical dystonia in 31%, upper limb jerky tremor in 63%, and head tremor in 59%, whereas generalized chorea was not a primary feature.

source.title: Bi-allelic ACBD6 variants lead to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with progressive and complex movement disorders
source.quote: The most conspicuous and common movement disorder was dystonia (94%), frequently leading to early-onset progressive postural deformities (97%), limb dystonia (55%) and cervical dystonia (31%). A jerky tremor in the upper limbs (63%), a mild head tremor (59%), parkinsonism/hypokinesia developing with advancing age (32%) and simple motor and vocal tics were among other frequent movement disorders.

evidence.text: A comprehensive review of hyperkinetic disorders in neurodevelopmental syndromes notes that corpus callosal agenesis suggests recessive ACBD6 mutations, where axial dystonia is reported in approximately 90% of cases.

source.title: Data‐Driven Insights into Hyperkinetic Disorders in Neurodevelopmental Syndromes and Epileptic Encephalopathies

new_directions.question_text: What proportion of ACBD6-associated jerky upper-limb movements represent true chorea versus jerky tremor, myoclonus, or dystonic jerks on quantitative surface electromyography?
new_directions.rationale: Review articles list ACBD6 under genetic chorea panels due to reports of 'chorea-like jerky movements', but precise electrophysiological phenotyping is necessary to disambiguate cortical/subcortical myoclonus, dystonic jerking, and true chorea.
